ideas.title: Zap a friend: static you carry
ideas.critique: This is the round 2 idea again, now naming the strand chains, the BEM equipotentials, Paschen for the gap and 1/2 CV^2. That answers the scripted-gag worry on paper, but a triboelectric column and a humidity leak rate are still lookups, and fibre-chain wool reacting to the solved field is a lot of work for the first step. What's strong is the form: a sneak-up the player plays, with the friends on the receiving end and a halo that grows by Coulomb's law. The island has never shown that, and people would replay it.

ideas.title: Copper from green water, on anything iron
ideas.nearest: A copper wire keeps its bends
same_form: A copper wire keeps its bends
ideas.critique: Cementation with Faraday thickness and thin-film tints is real chemistry, and a real second road to copper. But the dissolution and displacement rates will be constants fitted to look right. The film is a macro of a material's state creeping up, the same close-up form as the glass and the wire. Thin-film rainbow tints are a genuine Hikari showpiece, but 'dip it longer, thicker coat' is a progress bar, and friends bringing items is a delivery loop.

ideas.title: Lightning makes a lodestone
ideas.critique: This is round 2's idea with the striking-distance law and the 10/350 waveform from IEC 62305 put in. That makes attachment less tuned, but the cloud's charge layer is still a number someone sets, and fulgurite is still a melt threshold. It is the biggest shareable event on the list: a race against the storm with consequences you dig up afterwards. It leans on copper rods and a storm system that may not exist, and on several systems all landing in one session.

ideas.title: Treasure hunting with a needle
ideas.critique: A needle swinging over a hidden magnetic field has now been posted as the compass, the iron sticks and the putting tray. What this adds is that the player walks it and digs, and that walking shakes the needle, which is a real if small step. Ore bodies placed per seed, with magnetisations typed in, turn into a metal detector minigame with treasure placed in advance. The field solver answering 'where is the iron?' is honest, but it shows little that is new.
